title: Was Nagashino's Three-Row Volley Real? Who Added the 3,000 Matchlocks, Stroke by Stroke
description:
Tenshō 3, 5th month, 21st day (June 29, 1575 in the Julian calendar; July 9 in the Gregorian): at Nagashino in Mikawa, Oda and Tokugawa ashigaru crouch behind wooden fences built to stop horses, and across the field the Takeda army beats the drums to attack. For many people, the next picture is 3,000 matchlocks lined up in three rows, firing in turns: the "three-row volley" (sandan-uchi).

This episode follows that picture as it grew, layer by layer, in the order the records were written: Ōta Gyūichi's Shinchō Kōki only says "about 1,000 matchlocks," and the side that came on in turns was the Takeda; in the early Edo period, Oze Hoan's Shinchōki (usually dated to Genna 8, 1622, with 1604 and 1611 also proposed) makes it 3,000, a thousand per round, yet writes the last wave as a single all-out volley; a genealogy of the 1640s and the late-17th-century Sōkenki write in "taking turns" and "three relays" (mitsugawari); and in Meiji 36 (1903) the Army General Staff's Nihon Senshi: Nagashino-eki adds "3,000 picked from 10,000 gunners in the whole army," while the supplement of the same book quotes the Kōyō Gunkan: "horses charging the fence is a lie." Finally: how researchers have questioned it since 1980, the matchlock reenactments, and the Ikeda family copy and the folding screens that no one has yet checked in person.

The Shinchō Kōki is quoted from the Meiji-era Wagajikan Wagasho edition on Wikisource; Hoan's Shinchōki from the Genna 8 old movable-type edition and the Nihon Senshi: Nagashino-eki from the Meiji 36 edition, both in the National Diet Library Digital Collections. Most of the research history is secondhand, and each such source is marked in the references below.

The source of every quotation, year and number is listed in the references below; dates in the narration follow the old lunar calendar, and sentences beginning "we think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; the historical figures in them are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; modern researchers are not depicted.

Data as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten 2026-10-25 under new rules)

s101.text: 3,000 matchlocks, three rows: fire, drop back to reload, next row up.

s102.text: You've seen this picture: the standard answer for over 100 years.

s103.text: Tenshō 3, 5th month, 21st day: Nagashino, in Mikawa.

s104.text: Behind the fence an ashigaru crouches, gun in arms; opposite, Takeda drums beat.

s105.text: How many rows beside and behind him? The first book on that morning doesn't say a word.

s106.text: Not even the oddest part: that morning, one army really did come on in turns.

s107.text: Forty-odd years later, another man wrote up this battle; in the last wave, what did his matchlocks do?

s108.text: This file opens every book that wrote of these rows, in order, from Tenshō 3 to today.

s109.text: That morning, how did the matchlocks behind the fence fire?

s201.text: The first to write down how they fired was Ōta Gyūichi; his book is the Shinchō Kōki.

s202.text: As I said, he gave no rows; the gun count he did give: matchlocks, about 1,000.

s204.text: They went to five commanders, who had ashigaru close in step by step. Close in? Weren't they behind the fence?

s205.text: Another 500 crossed the river the night before with a unit, to raid Tobigasuyama.

s206.text: Count only the main line and it's this number; add the raid, and it's more.

s207.text: Nobunaga's roughly 30,000 men were hidden row on row in hollows, out of sight.

s208.text: Here's the catch: the Kōki's "rows" are about hiding troops, not firing.

s209.text: The Takeda had only about half as many men.

s210.text: At dawn, the first Takeda wave charged to drums.

s211.text: Wave one fell back, wave two came on; then the third, fourth and fifth.

s212.text: That army coming on in turns: which side?

s214.text: Gyūichi writes: from sunrise into the afternoon, wave after wave.

s215.text: The third wave: Kantō men, fine riders, set to charge in mounted.

s217.text: Not one main unit went out; just matchlocks and ashigaru.

s218.text: Our ashigaru behind the fence? Gyūichi writes: hide, fire when the enemy comes.

s220.text: He also noted an order: if the enemy charges, fall back; if it retreats, follow. He wrote both closing in and waiting.

s221.text: Strangely, read to the end, there are no groups, no swapping, no firing in turns.

s222.text: First time through, I reread it, afraid I'd missed something.

s223.text: By afternoon the Takeda pulled back, many senior vassals lost.

s224.text: So what about that 3,000? Is it in Gyūichi's book? Yes. Where?

s225.text: Five years before Nagashino: Genki 1, the fighting at Noda and Fukushima.

s226.text: Some 20,000 men from Kii, Negoro and Saika among them, reportedly brought just that many guns.

s227.text: Back then, they fought on Oda's side.

s228.text: For Gyūichi, those were someone else's guns. Who moved the number to Nagashino?

s301.text: The man who moved it was Oze Hoan.

s302.text: In early Edo, over 40 years after the battle, his Shinchōki was printed.

s303.text: Gyūichi's book stayed handwritten; Hoan's was printed and spread far wider.

s304.text: Say you had one nicely printed book and one hand copy: which would you open? Everyone chose the print.

s305.text: Yet a Tokugawa retainer of the same era wrote that it was full of lies.

s306.text: Hoan first: Katsuyori's men were all fine riders, so fences went up against horses.

s307.text: Gyūichi's fine riders were only the third wave; with Hoan, they became the whole army.

s308.text: Then the opening number appears: matchlocks drawn from every unit, 3,000,

s309.text: handed to the same five commanders.

s310.text: Order: no firing till they're within about 100 meters.

s311.text: Then a thousand at a time, row by row, in turns.

s313.text: Not in the book; readers worked it out themselves.

s314.text: Recall Gyūichi: when they charge, fall back; when they go, follow?

s315.text: Hoan reworked that passage, adding only the turns.

s316.text: Here's the catch: within one book, the number itself wobbles.

s317.text: First it's 3,000, a thousand a round; later, 3,000 each time, taking turns.

s318.text: Tokugawa's 300 matchlock ashigaru fight another way: each reloads, fires on.

s319.text: One battle, one book, three ways to fight. By here, I no longer knew which part to trust.

s320.text: In the fifth wave, the last Takeda unit charged.

s322.text: Hoan writes: once the enemy closed, over 2,000 matchlocks fired at once.

s323.text: The "three" even Hoan never wrote: who put it in later?

s401.text: Before the "three," a genealogy first changed one thing.

s402.text: In the 1640s, this daimyo genealogy gives Hoan's gun count; so what did it change?

s403.text: The five commanders took turns giving orders.

s405.text: The genealogy even has a line: when Toshiie's turn came.

s406.text: Mark the speed: in a generation or two, the number was in an official daimyo genealogy.

s407.text: Then the late-17th-century Sōkenki: what did it add?

s408.text: A thousand a turn, three turns.

s409.text: That's the earliest place we found the "three" spelled out.

s410.text: 110 years after that morning. I thought the three rows were complete by now,

s411.text: but how the rows stood, who fell back to reload: still nobody wrote it.

s412.text: It took over 200 more years, and the writer became a soldier.

s501.text: That soldier was the Japanese Army General Staff; in Meiji 36 they published Nihon Senshi: Nagashino-eki.

s502.text: They gave the opening number a source: 10,000 gunners in the whole army, 3,000 picked from them.

s503.text: Gyūichi never wrote these 10,000; nor did Hoan.

s504.text: The order follows suit: each thousand fires in turn.

s505.text: The book also calls Katsuyori "bold and reckless." You'd think the General Staff added that too?

s506.text: No. Edo war tales already wrote him that way: hot-blooded, deaf to old vassals.

s507.text: The Staff just made it official history.

s508.text: Stranger still, the same book's appendix quotes a Takeda military manual:

s509.text: Horses charging the fence is a lie; Nagashino's ground can't fit ten horses abreast.

s510.text: But Gyūichi's third wave plainly charged on horseback. The two don't match.

s511.text: Odd, isn't it: the book that made 3,000 official history undercuts itself in its appendix.

s512.text: And the opening image: front row fires, steps back to reload. In this book?

s513.text: No. Not even the General Staff wrote that.

s514.text: Researchers found the step-back-and-reload layer was added only after the Nihon Senshi.

s515.text: Historian Tokutomi Sohō copied it into his magnum opus; prewar scholars agreed.

s516.text: That 100-plus-year standard answer counts from this very book.

s517.text: A Japanese high-school textbook today: matchlock units beat Takeda's cavalry; no three rows.

s518.text: In all these years, did no one stand up and ask? Someone did. What did the first one ask?

s601.text: The first to ask was Fujimoto Masayuki.

s602.text: In 1980 he wrote an article whose title said it outright: Nagashino's matchlock tactics are fiction.

s603.text: He asked: who exactly, standing where, and how, could keep calling volleys for that many gunners?

s604.text: His answer: it can't be done. The Takeda lost, first of all, on numbers.

s605.text: He stressed those 500 too: once Tobigasuyama was raided, Katsuyori's retreat was cut; he could only charge head-on.

s606.text: Picture yourself behind the fence, smoke left and right: whose orders could you hear? My guess: nobody's.

s607.text: So could three men per group really fire in turns?

s608.text: Someone really tested a matchlock: one man loading and firing alone, about 20 seconds a shot.

s609.text: Three men taking turns, same six shots: about three times faster. Firing in turns works.

s610.text: In 2009, matchlock performers tried it on the old battlefield: four-man relay fire, three guns, six shots. And the whole line?

s611.text: One of the group said: in one corner of the field, maybe;

s612.text: a 2-km line all on command, with enough ammo? He can't picture it.

s613.text: Later another researcher measured the ground: under 100 paces wide, several fence lines, no room for three rows.

s614.text: Could do and did do are two different things. And the earliest book: is Gyūichi's the only copy?

s701.text: No. One copy of the Shinchō Kōki has a tiny "three" above and to the right of "thousand."

s703.text: Some say this copy is in Gyūichi's hand.

s704.text: Seen as added later, or his own fix.

s706.text: See? Even the earliest record has someone's added stroke; who, and in what year, no one can say for sure.

s707.text: What do the Edo-era Nagashino battle screens show?

s708.text: About ten such screens are known; Inuyama, Nagoya and the Tokugawa Art Museum each hold one.

s709.text: The museums say they show fences, matchlock units, and mounted warriors charging in.

s710.text: A report says they show no three-row volley. The catch: a painting can't show rows rotating;

s711.text: Nor have we seen these screens in person.

s712.text: If you ever stand before that screen, check one thing for me: is anyone behind the fence reloading?

s713.text: We think this picture lived so long because it turned a murky victory into one tidy diagram.

s714.text: Back to the opening question: that morning, how did the matchlocks behind the fence fire?

s715.text: Rows in turns were added later, stroke by stroke; but that no one fired in turns that day can't be proven either.

s717.text: What movie first showed you three rows firing in turns? Comment below.

s718.text: This channel tells only what records hold; subscribe to open files with us.
